title: RTX Spark Linux AI Performance Capped at 35% of Windows
summary: Nvidia RTX Spark laptops throttle GPU clocks to 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in, delivering only 35% of Windows AI inference speed due to encrypted firmware.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- RTX Spark laptops run AI models five times slower on native Linux than Windows when plugged in due to GPU clock throttling.
- Encrypted firmware power tables lock Linux GPU speeds at 780 MHz versus 2.2 GHz on Windows, dropping throughput from 65 to 14 tokens per second.
- WSL avoids the throttling bug and delivers near-Windows performance, making it the practical choice until Nvidia ships Linux driver fixes.


Nvidia's RTX Spark laptop delivers dramatically different AI performance depending on operating system. Benchmarks from MindStudio show the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus running GPT-OSS-120B at 65.4 tokens per second on Windows but only 13.9 tokens per second on native Linux when connected to power, roughly 35% of Windows throughput. The culprit is encrypted firmware that locks GPU clocks at 780 MHz on Linux versus 1.8 to 2.2 GHz on Windows, and no software workaround currently exists.


The RTX Spark platform ships in laptops including the MSI Prestige, Asus ProArt, and Dell XPS lines. These machines use the same GPU architecture as Nvidia's DGX Spark desktop but ship exclusively with Windows on ARM. Unlike the DGX Spark, which includes Nvidia's own Linux build out of the box, the laptop variants require manual Linux installation and driver configuration. The laptops support unified memory configurations up to 128GB shared between CPU and GPU, a feature marketed specifically at AI developers who typically rely on Linux-first tooling like vLLM and SGLang.


## Installation and Hardware Recognition


Installing Linux on the RTX Spark laptop requires multiple workarounds. An initial attempt using Omarchy Linux on the MSI Prestige produced an unstable, flickering display during boot. Switching to Debian provided a more stable foundation but lacked Wi-Fi drivers during installation, requiring a USB Ethernet adapter. The vanilla Debian kernel also failed to recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU without additional driver packages.


Returning to Omarchy resolved the driver problem because its kernel bundles Nvidia's open-source driver. However, Linux initially detected only 28GB of the laptop's 128GB unified memory because firmware reserves 96GB for GPU use by default. Adjusting the GPU memory allocation from Windows freed up 120GB for Linux to access. After these modifications, the laptop ran a full 4K desktop at 120Hz with working audio, input devices, and CUDA acceleration.


## The Performance Gap


Performance testing revealed a severe discrepancy between operating systems. Windows achieved 65.4 tokens per second with GPT-OSS-120B while native Linux managed only 13.9 tokens per second, a five-fold difference. WSL, which runs Linux inside Windows, hit 65.1 tokens per second, nearly identical to native Windows. The DGX Spark desktop running Nvidia's Linux build reached 61 tokens per second.


Extended benchmarks confirmed the pattern across different workloads:


- vLLM with eight concurrent clients: WSL reached 127 tokens per second, native Linux 39.5 tokens per second
- Sustained inference: Windows completed in 8 minutes at 2.2 GHz GPU clocks, Linux required 37 minutes at 790 MHz
- Temperatures remained between 40 and 47 degrees Celsius, ruling out thermal throttling


## Power Source Dependency


The throttling behavior reverses depending on power source. Running on battery, Linux achieved 61 to 67 tokens per second with LM Studio, comparable to Windows performance. GPU clocks reached approximately 1,800 MHz under load. When plugged into wall power, the same workload dropped to 15 tokens per second with clocks falling to 780 MHz. This counterintuitive pattern, worse performance when connected to power, distinguishes the issue from typical thermal or battery-saving throttling.


## Root Cause and Firmware Encryption


The problem traces to a component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework, visible in Windows Device Manager. This firmware and driver logic manages the shared power budget between CPU and GPU, necessary because laptops must balance power delivery between both chips rather than dedicating separate power rails. Disabling this controller in Windows reproduced the Linux slowdown directly, dropping performance from 83 to 31 tokens per second and GPU clocks from 2 GHz to 786 MHz. Re-enabling the controller immediately restored normal speed.


The deeper technical barrier is that firmware hands the controller an encrypted power table. Windows possesses the decryption key while Linux does not. Software attempts to bypass or decrypt the table on Linux, including one that triggered a kernel panic, failed to provide a general solution. Extracting the key from Windows drivers would create a fragile, machine-specific hack rather than a portable fix. A proper solution requires Nvidia to port the platform controller's power management logic into its Linux driver stack.


## WSL as the Practical Alternative


For most developers working with RTX Spark laptops today, WSL provides the most practical path forward. Because WSL runs on top of the Windows driver stack, it inherits Windows' full GPU boost behavior whether the laptop runs on battery or wall power. It supports Linux-native AI tools including vLLM and SGLang without encountering the clock throttling that affects bare-metal Linux installations.


The main adjustment needed is memory allocation. WSL reserves only 14GB by default, insufficient for large model workloads on a 128GB unified memory system. Manually increasing this allocation allows WSL benchmarks to match native Windows performance. This makes WSL the more reliable choice until Nvidia addresses the Linux driver gap directly.


## Officially Launched On


The RTX Spark laptop platform officially launched on November 4, 2026, shipping in MSI Prestige, Asus ProArt, and Dell XPS configurations. All variants ship with Windows on ARM and exhibit the same Linux throttling behavior when connected to wall power.


## What This Means


The RTX Spark laptop represents a significant hardware capability for on-device AI development with its unified memory architecture and ARM-based CUDA support. However, the encrypted firmware power management creates a hard ceiling for native Linux performance that software cannot currently overcome. Developers who require Linux environments can achieve near-Windows performance using WSL, but those who need bare-metal Linux for containerization, kernel development, or other use cases face a choice between accepting severely degraded performance or waiting for Nvidia to ship the necessary driver components. The situation highlights the ongoing challenges of hardware vendor support for Linux in mobile AI workstations, particularly when firmware-level power management intersects with new platform architectures.
